levelMapping: Atlassian ladder: P30 = early-career SWE, P40 = 'Software Engineer II' / SDE-2 (≈ Google L4, Amazon SDE II), P50 = Senior Software Engineer (≈ L5), P60 = Principal. Older posts write P3/P4/P5 for the same bands. With ~3.3 YOE the realistic band is P40: 2025–26 India P40 offers went to candidates with 4–6 YOE, and 6–7 YOE candidates interviewing for P50 were routinely down-levelled to P40 after the loop (panel judges 'needs guidance to operate as a senior'). Interview loops are identical for P40 and P50; P50 adds depth/expectation in system design and the management round, and P60 adds a leadership-craft round. Ask the recruiter to confirm the band up front — the hiring committee can also offer one level lower than you interviewed for.

process.summary: Atlassian runs a company-wide, team-agnostic loop for backend P40/P50: recruiter screen → 60-min outsourced Karat screen (rapid-fire system-design scenarios + 1–2 DSA problems) → 'Stage 1' of two 60-min coding interviews (Data Structures, and Code Design/LLD) → 'Stage 2' of System Design (60), Management/'how you work' (60) and Values (45) → hiring committee → team matching → offer. Each stage is eliminatory and feedback is given as Hire/No-Hire with confidence per round. The coding rounds are machine-coding style on your own IDE with tests expected, and Atlassian is notorious for reusing a small bank of questions (snake game, rate limiter, agent ratings, tagging service, employee-directory LCA), so past write-ups are unusually predictive. Values and Management rounds carry real weight — several 2025 candidates with Hire in every technical round were rejected or down-levelled on Values.

rounds.name: Recruiter / exploratory call
rounds.what: Background, why switching, compensation expectations, which band (P40/P50) you are being considered for, walkthrough of the loop. Recruiter emails a prep guide (role-specific 'candidate guide' PDF) and usually gives ~2 weeks before the first round.
rounds.probes: Current tech stack vs. role stack; notice period; location/band (India band pays on India scale).

rounds.name: Karat technical screen (pre-interview test)
rounds.what: Outsourced to Karat (interviewer is a Karat 'Interview Engineer', not an Atlassian engineer; recorded). ~3 min intro, then ~20 min of 4–5 rapid-fire system-design/debugging scenarios (~4 min each, verbal only, no diagrams), then ~30 min with two DSA problems (one easy, one medium) in Karat's browser editor (Coderbyte/Karat Studio, 5–7 test cases per problem; Google allowed per several reports). Frontend/fullstack variant replaces DSA with HTML/CSS + vanilla-JS DOM tasks. Reported pass bar (2023–2025 India reports): fully solve ≥1 coding problem and explain an approach for the second, and get ~3/5 of the rapid-fire scenarios right (one candidate was told the rapid-fire pass mark was 3 of 5). A guide estimates ~50–60% of Karat takers advance; common fails are not comparing multiple approaches and slow reasoning on the scenarios. One redo is allowed and the better attempt counts (Karat may auto-cancel the redo if you already passed). Results typically arrive in 1–3 business days.
rounds.probes: Rapid-fire scenarios seen 2025: consistent hashing by file-count for music servers (problems + fix); capacity estimation for an ML URL-parsing service over 6 months; file larger than one machine's RAM; going from one country to many; preload vs. server-fetch puzzle hints; friend-count on posts from User/UserRelationship tables at > Facebook scale; Google-Docs-like docs pinned to servers by round-robin — what breaks; strong vs. eventual consistency for video-metadata API / click analytics / banking; find request IDs missing from 500 servers' success logs (lost e-signature notifications); throughput of a 3-stage pipeline with capacities 10/20/50; walk through 'confirm ride' end to end; debugging a slow system; scaling x→y users.

rounds.name: Data Structures interview (Stage 1, coding #1)
rounds.what: One real-world-framed problem that unfolds in 2–4 stages (the interviewer adds requirements), solved in your own IDE in any language with tests you write. Expect to construct the data model first (e.g. build the org-hierarchy graph before finding the LCA). Topics skew to hash maps, heaps/TreeMaps, intervals/sweep line, trees/LCA, Dijkstra, and 'design a data structure' problems (All O'one / Stock Price Fluctuation style).
rounds.probes: Clarifying questions before coding (explicit No-Hire reason in a Jan 2025 debrief), edge cases such as a non-existent employee, correct time/space complexity, why DFS/BFS won't do (Dijkstra), tie-breaking rules, concurrency (how would this behave with writers in other threads), and reaching the 'level 2' extension in time. Code quality and naming are scored here too, not only correctness.

rounds.name: Code Design interview (Stage 1, coding #2, a.k.a. LLD / machine coding)
rounds.what: Build a small working system from a short spec, production-quality: classes/interfaces, SOLID, extensibility, exception handling and unit tests (recruiter prep guide explicitly suggests TDD). Historically on your own IDE/HackerRank CodePair; Atlassian's 2026 backend candidate guide (as read by third parties) describes the Code Design round as 'AI-enabled' — working in a HackerRank IDE with an AI assistant on an existing repository (add a feature / fix a bug / refactor), with testing part of the grade. 2026 reports mention 'fix a password bug in a small backend site' and MERN-project tasks, but the classic bank (snake game, rate limiter, agent ratings, cost explorer, router) was still being asked through 2025–Jan 2026.
rounds.probes: Write the requirements as comments first; the follow-up stages (burst credits, per-month ratings, wildcard routes, trial periods, toroidal walls) test whether the first design was extensible. Debrief feedback cited 'no unit tests', 'no exception handling', 'corner cases not covered', 'did not justify approach', 'no logging or locks' as No-Hire reasons. Data-structure choice must be justified (deque vs linked list, list vs set, TreeMap vs heap).

rounds.name: System Design interview (Stage 2)
rounds.what: One Jira/Confluence-flavoured HLD problem on a whiteboard tool, starting from functional requirements and escalating. The tagging service is asked so often that Blind posters say 'everyone gets this'. Interviewers go unusually deep on API contracts (request/response JSON, pagination) and DB schema before scaling.
rounds.probes: API spec, DB schema and SQL-vs-NoSQL choice, per-user filtering/ranking schema, queue choice (SQS vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka), rate limiting, which component bottlenecks first and how to scale it, consistency, failure handling/retries for crawler jobs, time-window queries, real-time updates. At P40 a 'rushed' design still got Hire-low-confidence; at P50 expect capacity estimation and failure modes unprompted.

rounds.name: Management / 'How you work' interview (hiring-manager style)
rounds.what: Structured, scenario-based behavioural interview with an engineering manager (often not your eventual manager — team match comes later). Deep dive into one project you owned end to end, plus how your team plans, gathers requirements, tests and collaborates.
rounds.probes: Owning a project end to end; handling vague requirements; scope expanding mid-project; pushing back on a colleague or senior engineer's decision; a team-mate repeatedly missing commitments; mentoring/helping someone grow; conflict with a manager; SDLC and how you split work among peers; why X over Y, what you learned, what you'd do differently. Weak leadership examples have caused 'Weak Hire/No Hire' here even with strong technicals.

rounds.name: Values interview
rounds.what: Interviewer from outside the hiring team asks roughly one STAR question per Atlassian value — 'Open company, no bullshit', 'Build with heart and balance', 'Don't #@!% the customer', 'Play, as a team', 'Be the change you seek' — each with 2–3 scenario follow-ups. Questions are indirect (they rarely name the value).
rounds.probes: Time you initiated change at a company; mentoring someone; handling a conflict / giving hard feedback to a senior stakeholder; shipping a customer-facing bug and what you did; a project being deprioritised; putting the customer over short-term business interest; disagreeing with a lead's architecture decision. Clarify whether a question has one or two parts — one candidate was marked down for answering only option A of 'A or B'. A No-Hire here overrides Hire in all five other rounds.

rounds.name: Hiring committee, team matching, offer
rounds.what: Interviewers' written feedback goes to a hiring committee separate from the panel, which decides hire and the level (down-levels P50→P40 are common; HC rejections despite all-Hire feedback were reported in Jul 2025). Then 1–2 team-matching calls with hiring managers, then offer. Headcount can disappear mid-loop ('positions filled, we'll keep you warm 2–3 weeks').
rounds.probes: Team-match calls are conversational (project interests, team's stack); negotiation with competing offers (Microsoft) worked for India P40 candidates.

process.indiaNotes: Bengaluru is Atlassian's main India engineering hub and hires heavily at P30/P40/P50 (remote-in-India roles exist too); the loop and the question bank are identical to US/ANZ — several India candidates were interviewed by Sydney panels and vice versa, and EU applicants have had their code-design round run by the India team. Differences: (1) comp is on the India band — reported 2025–Jan 2026 P40 offers were ₹47–58L base + ₹6.5L joining + 14–15% bonus + US$100–105k RSUs/4 yrs (≈₹78–100L TC yr 1); P50 India offers were ₹65–84L base + US$115–160k RSUs; (2) timelines in India ran ~6 weeks (Day 0 recruiter → Day 41 offer in one Aug 2025 report) but HC/headcount approvals stretched some loops to 2 months, and Dec–Jan hiring slows; (3) India candidates report more down-levelling P50→P40 and 'positions filled' holds; (4) on-campus India hiring uses a HackerRank OA (90 min, 3 problems) and, in 2026, an 'AI-enabled' debug-a-repo round — not relevant to lateral P40. Interviewers are frequently P40/P50 engineers from Bangalore teams (Jira Search, Cloud Migrations, Confluence).
process.timeline: Typically 4–8 weeks end to end: Karat within a week of recruiter call; Stage 1 (two coding rounds, often same or consecutive days) a week later; Stage 2 (design + management + values) over the following 1–2 weeks; HC decision 1–4 weeks; team matching ~1 week; written offer ~1 week after verbal. Fastest India report: 41 days contact→offer; slowest: ~2 months with a month waiting on HC.
tips: Treat the public question bank as the syllabus: snake game, per-customer rate limiter (+ credit/burst follow-up), support-agent ratings (+ per-month, tie-break, weighted), cost explorer, middleware router, employee-directory LCA, popularity tracker, files/collections top-N, tagging service, Confluence top-K feed, image crawler. 2025–26 candidates repeatedly say 'most questions came from LeetCode Discuss'.

In both coding rounds: write the requirements as comments, ask clarifying questions before typing, state complexity correctly, handle invalid input, and finish with runnable unit tests — every No-Hire debrief quoted one of these.
Practise Code Design under a 45-minute clock; multiple strong engineers ran 5–10 minutes over on snake game. Aim for a working core in ~25 minutes so the extension stage gets reached.

Design rounds reward API-first depth: write the endpoint list with request/response bodies and the table schema early, then scale. Confirm ambiguous metrics (what counts as 'engagement'/'popular') in the first 5 minutes.

Karat: ask the interviewer not to read the scenario text aloud (saves time in the 20-min rapid-fire), give a quick 'concern → fix' answer per scenario, and move on; one fully solved coding problem plus a clear approach for the second has been enough to pass.

Prepare 8–10 STAR stories mapped to the five values plus 'owned end to end', 'scope changed', 'pushed back', 'mentored'; Values/Management are graded as hard as the technical rounds and are the most common reason strong candidates fail.
Expect follow-ups that change the problem (variable increments, tie-break strategy, time windows, concurrency); design the first version so these are additive.
If the recruiter mentions AI-enabled Code Design, practise reading an unfamiliar small repo, adding a feature with tests, and narrating what you accept or reject from the assistant.
process.notes: Pre-interview test: Karat (60 min, format above) for backend/fullstack laterals; a Feb 2026 Blind thread says some roles (P50 phone screen) moved off Karat to an Atlassian-run screen with the same shape (~20 min coding + ~15 min system design); a Feb 2025 US SF loop used a HackerRank OA (2–3 medium-hard) instead. Karat redo: one retake, best score counts. Coding rounds: any language, own IDE and test framework (CodePair fallback); Google allowed in Karat per reports. Code Design round is being migrated to an AI-enabled HackerRank IDE on an existing repo (2026 candidate guide) — confirm with your recruiter which variant you'll get. Feedback vocabulary: Strong Hire / Hire (high|medium|low confidence) / No Hire per round, with level recommendation (e.g. 'Hire at P40, P50 for system design'). Hiring is to the company, then team match; roles can close mid-loop. Cool-off after rejection is reportedly ~6–12 months (recruiter-stated, not verified here). Frontend/fullstack loops swap the DS round for JS/React rounds and may add a 'Fullstack Craft' project walkthrough; SRE-flavoured teams can add an 'SRE Craft' round at team match.

dsa.title: Closest common group in an employee directory (LCA on an org hierarchy)
dsa.statement: You are given an organisation hierarchy: the company is the root, groups/departments contain sub-groups and employees are leaves. Stage (a): build the structure from the input and return the closest (deepest) group that contains every employee in a given target set. Stage (b): groups can be shared or an employee can sit in several groups, so the structure is a DAG — still return one closest common group. Stage (c): four mutation methods run on other threads while getCommonGroupForEmployees is called; keep results consistent with the latest hierarchy (read-write lock discussion). Stage (d) simplification: a single level of groups.
dsa.variant: Asked as 'closest department for a list of employees' and 'LCA of a pair of leaves in an n-ary tree'. Interviewers push for a more efficient LCA than naive root-paths (precompute depth/parent pointers, or walk up from the deepest node) and insist you handle a non-existent employee; the Jan 2025 No-Hire cited no clarifying questions, a missed edge case and a wrong complexity.
dsa.evidence: Reported in at least 5 Data Structures rounds: P50 Jan 2025, P50 Jul–Aug 2025, P40 Bangalore Sept 2025 (n-ary pair-of-leaves form), P60 Sept 2025, plus the Aug 2025 'DS question bank' post with all four stages. The single most repeated Atlassian DSA question of 2025.

dsa.title: Popularity tracker: increasePopularity / decreasePopularity / getMostPopular
dsa.statement: Stream of content IDs with +1 / -1 popularity events; return the most popular ID at any time (or -1 when nothing is above 0). Same shape as All O'one.
dsa.variant: Follow-ups reported: change popularity by an arbitrary amount x instead of 1 (breaks the O(1) bucket trick — discuss TreeMap/heap with lazy deletion), tie-breaking strategy when several IDs share the max, and thread-safety. Also framed as 'incPop/decPop/getMostPop for tags' and as a Principal LLD 'most popular content with thumbs-up/down counts'.
dsa.evidence: P40 Aug 2025 (DSA round, Hire high-confidence), SDE-2 2025 Medium write-up (DSA round, Hire), Principal Bengaluru Sept 2025 (LLD round), Blind code-design bank, Aug 2025 DS bank post.

dsa.title: Support-agent ratings: record 1–5 ratings, list agents sorted by average
dsa.statement: Implement addAgentRating(agentId, rating) and getSortedAgentRatingsList() for a customer-support tool: maintain each agent's running sum/count and return all agents ordered by average rating, highest first, with a defined tie-break.
dsa.variant: Stages reported: (b) add month-aware ratings and return the best agents for a given month; (c) tie-breaking (more ratings wins / agent id); (d) weighted votes; (e) concurrency with many raters. Often graded as the Code Design round, but has also been asked as the DSA round, and candidates were expected to use TDD. Appears in LLD list too — practise it as code.
dsa.evidence: Reported at least 7 times Nov 2024–Jan 2026: P40 India Aug 2025 (code design), P40 Aug 2025 Hold (code design), P50 Jul–Aug 2025 (code design), Senior Eng coding round (weighted-votes follow-up), SWE Jan 2026 coding round (no follow-up asked), Blind May 2025 and Nov 2025 LLD posts.

dsa.title: Stock Price Fluctuation / commodity price at a timestamp
dsa.variant: Atlassian variant: a stream of <timestamp, price> records arriving out of order and possibly repeating a timestamp (upsert the price); support getMaxCommodityPrice at any time, optimised for frequent reads and writes. Follow-ups: 'highest price at a given timestamp' and a checkpoint variant — after each insert a checkpoint is placed; given a timestamp and a checkpoint, return the max price up to that point (think persistent/segment structure or per-checkpoint snapshots).
dsa.evidence: SDE-2 backend Jul 2025 (DSA round, Strong Hire), SDE2 reject post (checkpoint follow-up), Aug 2025 DS bank post ('Commodity Prices').

dsa.title: Merge Intervals / overlapping time series
dsa.variant: Jan 2026 P40 report: merge-intervals with different wording, then follow-ups that required a sweep-line (count overlaps / find the busiest instant). Aug 2025 Glassdoor: 'discover overlapping time series from a set of start and end times' asked in the first round and the candidate was rejected for not knowing the sweep approach. Overlapping booking slots variant also reported.
dsa.evidence: P40 Jan 2026 DSA round (Hire, high confidence); Senior SWE Aug 2025 Glassdoor; Dataford question list; interviewing reports mention interval problems repeatedly.

dsa.title: Tennis court booking: assign bookings to the minimum number of courts
dsa.variant: Atlassian framing: BookingRecord{id, start, finish}; return a plan mapping each booking to a court using the fewest courts (unlimited courts). Stages: (b) each court needs a fixed maintenance gap X after every booking; (c) maintenance Y only after every X uses ('durability'); (d) simplified — just return the minimum number of courts; (e) helper that says whether two bookings conflict. Min-heap on court free-time.
dsa.evidence: Aug 2025 DS question-bank post (all five stages), Dataford 'tennis court booking' LLD entry, GetSDEReady list.

dsa.title: Cinema scheduling: can a new movie be scheduled without removing existing shows?
dsa.statement: A single-screen cinema is open 10:00–23:00 on one day; times are minutes from midnight. Given existing screenings (movie, start) and movie durations, implement canSchedule(movie, schedule) that returns whether the new movie's duration fits in some free gap (including before the first and after the last show, within opening hours). Sample data: LOTR 120 min at 660/840/1200, Back to the Future 90 min at 1020.
dsa.variant: Natural extensions: return the earliest feasible start, multiple screens, cleaning buffers between shows.
dsa.evidence: P60 Sept 2025 code-design round; GetSDEReady list ('Cinema Scheduling 10 AM–11 PM').

dsa.title: Minimum latency between services (Dijkstra on a weighted service graph)
dsa.variant: Given N connected services with latency-weighted edges, answer Q queries for the minimum latency from service X to Y. Interviewer discussed why BFS/DFS are unsuitable, how Dijkstra works, alternatives (Floyd–Warshall / precomputation for many queries) and complexity.
dsa.evidence: P40 India Aug 2025 Data Structures round (Hire, medium confidence); GetSDEReady list.

dsa.title: Files and collections: total size and top-N collections by size
dsa.variant: Atlassian framing: each file has a name, size and optional collectionId; produce a report with the total size of all files and the top N collections by total size. Stages: files belonging to multiple collections; nested collections (roll sizes up the tree); multithreaded ingestion. Sometimes labelled 'file storage system' and run as the DSA pair-programming round.
dsa.evidence: Senior SWE offer (Dec 2024) Data Structures round; SDE-2 remote accepted (nested-collections follow-up); SDE2 P4 Bengaluru Mar 2025 (coding round 2, with List-vs-Set and time/space follow-ups); Glassdoor Melbourne 6-round loop ('design a file storage system', DSA pair-programming).

dsa.title: Rank Teams by Votes / ballot ranking with custom tie-break
dsa.variant: Variants: positional weights per ballot, a different tie-break rule than LeetCode's, interviewer changing requirements twice mid-round; the clean solution needed Ballot/Candidate classes and a comparator. Simpler form: given a vote stream {c1,c2,c1,...} return the winner and discuss tie-break strategies (earliest to reach the count, fewest later votes, weighted).
dsa.evidence: Senior SWE Nov 2023 DS round (Gagandeep), 2023 experience with different tie-break, backend 3 YOE Bangalore 2021, voting-application question post, Blind bank 'voting system' variants, TechPrep list.

dsa.title: Online Election / live leader of a vote stream
dsa.variant: Interviewer started with basic requirements (who is leading now) and layered complexity (leader at time t, ties resolved by most recent vote). Related to the voting-system family.
dsa.evidence: P5 Bengaluru May 2021 coding round 2 (offer); still listed in 2025 question banks as 'Voting System (live leader)'.

dsa.title: Grocery shopping: department visits saved by grouping purchases
dsa.statement: Given a catalogue of (product → department) and a shopping list in purchase order, count a 'department visit' each time the department changes from the previous item. Return how many visits you save by buying everything in one department before moving to the next (i.e. in-order visits minus distinct departments). Example: [Blueberries, Milk, Coffee, Flour, Cheese, Carrots] → 5 in-order visits vs 3 grouped → answer 2.
dsa.variant: Phone-screen style problem with a provided test table; follow-ups likely on unknown products and preserving first-visit order.
dsa.evidence: Atlassian technical phone screen, Oct 2025.

dsa.title: Office attendance violations (consecutive enter/enter or exit/exit)
dsa.statement: Attendance records are [name, 'enter'|'exit'] pairs in time order. Correct behaviour alternates enter→exit. Return two lists: names with an entry violation (two enters in a row) and names with an exit violation (two exits in a row), each name at most once, in order of first violation.
dsa.variant: Karat coding problem (second part of the screen); typical Karat follow-up adds a second part such as counting violations per person or handling a missing final exit.
dsa.evidence: Karat screen for P50 band, Aug 2025.

dsa.title: Board game with teleporters: positions reachable with one die roll / can the end be reached
dsa.statement: A board is numbered 0..lastNumber with a start position, a die with faces 1..maxValue and teleporters given as 'from,to' strings. A roll past lastNumber lands on lastNumber. Part 1 (code): return all distinct final positions after exactly one roll (apply teleporters). Part 2 (approach only): decide whether lastNumber is reachable in any number of rolls (BFS over positions).
dsa.variant: Karat two-part problem; cycles via backward teleporters must be handled with a visited set.
dsa.evidence: Karat screen for P40, Mar 2025.

dsa.title: Text Justification variant
dsa.variant: Karat coding problem 'similar to LC 68' with one follow-up (candidate solved main part fully and described the follow-up). Word-wrap problem also listed in question banks.
dsa.evidence: P40 India Aug 2025 Karat screen; appears in the LeetCode Atlassian tag.

dsa.title: Two Sum variation (Karat warm-up)
dsa.variant: Karat first coding problem is frequently an easy variation (pairs summing to a target with constraints); the second problem was BFS-based and only the approach was discussed because time ran out.
dsa.evidence: P50 Jul–Aug 2025 Karat screen.

dsa.title: Form a word from a dictionary word (letters multiset) — Karat
dsa.statement: Given a word list such as [baby, cat, dada, dog] and a query string, return the dictionary word whose letters can be formed from the query's letters without reusing a character ('ctay' → 'cat'; 'dad' → '-' because dada needs two d's and two a's). About 8 provided test cases. Second part (approach only): given a 2-D character grid, decide whether a word exists moving only down or right.
dsa.variant: Second part is a constrained Word Search (LC 79) — DP/DFS with right/down moves only.
dsa.evidence: Senior SWE offer loop (Karat, Dec 2024) and Senior Backend SWE Glassdoor Jan 2025 (same 'form a word without reusing characters' problem).

dsa.title: Word Search (grid) — right/down-only approach discussion
dsa.variant: Karat part-2 'approach only' question: word exists in a character matrix moving only down or right. LeetCode Atlassian tag ranks Word Search in the top 5 for 2026.
dsa.evidence: Senior SWE Karat screen (Dec 2024); LC company tag.

dsa.title: Middleware router: addRoute(path, result) / callRoute(path) with wildcards
dsa.statement: Implement a router where paths map to results (stand-ins for handlers): addRoute('/bar','result'); callRoute('/bar') → 'result'. Follow-up: wildcard segments — addRoute('/bar/*/baz','bar') must match callRoute('/bar/a/baz'). Then resolve ambiguity between '/foo/baz' and '/foo/*' for callRoute('/foo/baz') (prefer exact over wildcard; define priority) and discuss path parameters.
dsa.variant: Graded as Code Design; rejection feedback demanded justification of the trie choice plus logging/locks. Also surfaces as 'Design File System (LC 1166) with * and ? wildcards in createPath/get'.
dsa.evidence: SDE2 reject post (code design round); 2023 experience (LC 1166 + wildcards); Glassdoor 'design a sample router' (Senior SWE); Blind Nov 2025 'trie' coding round complaint; Dataford list.

dsa.title: Design File System with wildcard paths
dsa.variant: Follow-up: support * and ? in createPath so get('/a/x/y/b') returns the value stored for '/a/*/b'; interviewer suggested pattern matching inside createPath.
dsa.evidence: 2023 LeetCode experience; LC Atlassian tag.

dsa.title: Sub-list search (find index of list B inside list A) → KMP
dsa.variant: Given two lists, return the 0-based start index where the second appears contiguously in the first, else -1: (2,3) in (1,2,3) → 1; (3,2) → -1. Follow-up: make it fast enough with KMP.
